ز کیخسرو این یاد ماند از جهان
که تاج است رفتنی، بماند داستان

27.title: Part 27: Goshtasp and the Coming of Zoroaster
27.prose:
After Kay Khusrow withdrew from the world and Lohrasp took the throne, the age of the Kayanids entered a new phase. Lohrasp began his reign, but among his sons and successors, Goshtasp became especially important to Iran’s future. Goshtasp was ambitious and strong, and because his future claim to the throne seemed uncertain, he came into conflict with his father.

The dispute eventually drove Goshtasp away from Iran. He traveled toward Rome and came to a land where he met Katayun, the daughter of the Roman Caesar. Contrary to the expectations of the court, Katayun chose Goshtasp, and their union prepared the way for his return to Iran and the strengthening of his position. After his return, Goshtasp once again entered the center of power, and his fate became bound to the future of the Iranian empire.

In this same period, a great event took place in Iran’s culture and religion: Zoroaster came to Goshtasp with a new message and faith. In the Shahnameh’s account, he called people to the path of truth, justice, purity, and avoidance of falsehood. Zoroaster’s coming was not merely a change in religious belief; within the epic story, it marked the beginning of an era in which Goshtasp’s kingship became bound to a new faith and its defense.

Goshtasp accepted this faith, and a number of nobles joined him. The new religion did not please everyone. Resistance arose at court and among opposing political forces, while the hostility of Arjasp, king of Turan, intensified. In his eyes, the change of faith in Iran was not merely a religious matter; it signaled a political and cultural transformation that could alter the balance between Iran and Turan.

To establish the new faith, Goshtasp needed the support of his family and champions. Zarir, his brother, became one of the first great defenders and warriors of this period. Soon Esfandiyar, Goshtasp’s son, also emerged as the most important military figure of the family—a champion who would play a decisive role both in defending Iran and in Goshtasp’s own fate.

Meanwhile, Arjasp was preparing to confront Iran. The acceptance of the new faith became a pretext for new wars, followed by threatening messages and Turanian campaigns. Thus religious transformation became linked to a major political and military confrontation, and Iran once again stood against Turan.

At this stage Goshtasp is more than the king of a country. He stands where the Kayanid royal tradition meets a new faith and a new generation of champions. From this point, Zarir and especially Esfandiyar move to the center of the story, and the struggle with Arjasp lays the groundwork for one of the Shahnameh’s great later tragedies. Goshtasp’s story is therefore a bridge between the age of Kay Khusrow and the world of Esfandiyar, a world in which religion, power, family, and war become increasingly intertwined.
27.originalVerse:
به تخت اندر آمد ز گشتاسپ نام
ز لهراسپ بردند تخت و مقام

چو گشتاسپ دید آن ره پُر ز بیم
دلش خواست آیین و رای و ندیم

ز روم آمد آن شاهزادهٔ دلیر
به ایران درآمد به کردار شیر

کتایون چو دیدش دلش شد گرو
که بود از نژاد بزرگی نکو

ز دانایی آمد پیام‌آورِ دین
سخن گفت از راه داد و یقین

گشتاسپ پذیرفت آن راه نو
که بر راستی بود و دور از بدی رو

چو آیین نو در جهان آشکار
شدند از پی‌اش مردمانِ بسیار

ز توران برآمد خروش نبرد
که آیین نو کینه‌ها برانگیخت

زریر آمد آن نامور پهلوان
به پشتیبانی ز شاه جهان

اسفندیار آن جوانِ نامدار
شد امید گشتاسپ در روزگار

28.title: Part 28: The War Between Iran and Turan and Arjasp
28.prose:
Goshtasp’s acceptance of Zoroaster’s faith was not merely a change within the Iranian court; in the world of the Shahnameh, it also provoked Iran’s enemies. Arjasp, king of Turan, grew angry at the spread of the new faith and condemned Goshtasp for the change. When he received Goshtasp’s reply, threats turned into a military campaign, and once again the borders of Iran and Turan stood on the brink of war.

Arjasp assembled a great army and marched toward Iran. His aim was not merely to defeat a king; he wanted to crush the new political and cultural force that had taken shape in Iran. The Turanian army approached Iranian lands, and cities and religious centers came under threat. Goshtasp was forced to prepare his army and defend both his country and the new faith.

Among the Iranians, Zarir, Goshtasp’s brother, was among the first to bear the burden of war. He was an experienced and loyal champion and led the Iranian army in battle. The opening clashes were fierce and bloody, and both sides suffered heavy losses. The war was no longer a simple confrontation between two kings; many families and champions were drawn into it, and Iran’s fate depended on their courage.

In one of the great battles, Zarir fought with extraordinary bravery, but was eventually killed. His death dealt a heavy blow to Goshtasp and the Iranian army. Yet the defeat and death of the champions did not completely destroy the Iranians’ strength and resolve. On the contrary, Zarir’s death became a sign of the high price of defending Iran and brought a new generation of warriors into the field.

In this period Esfandiyar rose ever more prominently. He was Goshtasp’s son and one of the strongest champions of his generation. Esfandiyar was loyal to the new faith and possessed great military ability. After the death of Zarir and other heroes, attention turned increasingly toward him, and Goshtasp realized that continuing the war with Turan would be difficult without Esfandiyar’s strength.

The war between Iran and Turan took on a long and exhausting character. Every victory came with a new wound, and every defeat revealed the need for another champion. The Turanians also possessed great warriors, and Arjasp was not easily driven back. As a result, the frontier between the two countries repeatedly became a battlefield.

But the importance of this war lies not only in the outcome of its battles. With Zarir’s death and Esfandiyar’s emergence, a new generation of the epic enters the center of the story. From this point onward, Esfandiyar will be not merely a young prince but one of the principal pillars of Iran’s defense—a champion whose fate will eventually place him before his father’s most difficult command: to confront Rustam.
28.originalVerse:
چو ارجاسپ بر مرز ایران رسید
خروش سپه در جهان دردمید

گشتاسپ ز بهر کشور سپاه

زریر آن یل نامور پیش رفت
به میدان چو شیر ژیان خویش رفت

ز شمشیر او دشمنان در گریخت
ولی بخت گردان به ناگاه ریخت

چو زریر افتاد در خون و خاک
دل شاه و گردان شد از درد چاک

اسفندیار آمد آن نامدار
به میدان و شد تکیه‌گاهِ سوار

ز پسِ مرگ یل‌های نام‌آوران
شد او امیدِ ایران و جنگاوران

ز ایران و توران برآمد خروش
که از رزم ماندست گردون به جوش

چنین جنگ‌ها نسل‌ها را کشید
و نام دلیران به گیتی رسید

29.title: Part 29: Esfandiyar’s Seven Labors
29.prose:
To free his daughters Homay and Beh-Afarid, who were imprisoned in the Turanian fortress of Ruyin-Dezh, Goshtasp sent Esfandiyar on a difficult journey. On the surface, the mission was an opportunity to prove his valor, but beneath it lay the continuing conflict between father and son: Goshtasp had a great champion before him, yet still feared making him his successor. Esfandiyar was forced to enter a land whose passage was far from easy.

Esfandiyar set out from Iran with an army, but he did not choose the direct route. Instead he passed through the path that the Shahnameh made famous as the Seven Labors. Each labor was a separate trial, confronting the champion with a new danger. First came the desert, thirst, and the hardship of the journey; then wild beasts and enemies lying in wait tested his physical strength and resolve. In one of the labors, wolves, lions, and powerful creatures blocked his path, and Esfandiyar passed them through strength and endurance.

Later, a fearsome dragon blocked the road. The struggle was not merely a test of power; it required awareness and timing. Through wisdom and courage, Esfandiyar overcame this danger as well. He then encountered a sorceress who tried to turn him from his path through deception and trickery. Esfandiyar was not deceived by appearances and recognized the truth of the enemy. After that, the road toward the enemy’s land opened further, and through perseverance and command he brought his army close to Ruyin-Dezh.

Esfandiyar’s Seven Labors are not merely a collection of heroic battles. In this journey he becomes more fully known as a champion who possesses both martial strength and the ability to decide in moments of danger. He emerges from each labor with new experience and moves toward a fortress where freeing his sisters and breaking the enemy’s power will be the next stage of his mission. At last Esfandiyar approached Ruyin-Dezh and prepared for the battle that would place his name among the greatest champions of the new generation.
29.originalVerse:
اسفندیار آمد به راه دراز
دلش پر ز بیم و نهان بی‌نیاز
ز هفت‌خوان گذشت آن یل نامدار
به شمشیر و تدبیر و عزم استوار
نخستین رهش تشنگی بود و رنج
پس از آن برآمد ز هر سو گزند
ز گرگ و ز شیر و ز دیو و اژدها
همی آزمودند مردی و را
چو جادوی بدخواه بر راه دید
ز نیرنگ او نیز روی برتافت
به رویین‌دژ آمد دلیر و جوان
که پیروز گردد به رزم گران
همای و به‌آفرید در بند اوست
رهِ رزم و پیروزی از پیش اوست

30.title: Part 30: The Opening of the Invulnerable Fortress
30.prose:
After passing the Seven Labors, Esfandiyar reached Turan and made his way to the Invulnerable Fortress, a stronghold renowned for its strength and impenetrability, which for years had kept enemies from approaching. Inside the fortress, Homay and Beh-Afarid, Esfandiyar’s sisters, were held captive, and freeing them was one of the chief aims of his campaign.

Esfandiyar knew that a direct assault could inflict heavy losses on the Iranian army. Before beginning the battle, therefore, he turned to strategy and careful planning. He sought a way to approach the fortress and, at last, through a suitable disguise and a calculated plan, found a means of entering its walls. This part of the story shows that heroism is not merely a matter of physical strength: sometimes victory comes through wisdom and an understanding of circumstances.

Once the way was opened, fighting began inside the Invulnerable Fortress. Its defenders fought with all their strength, but Esfandiyar and his army overcame them. The walls that had for years been a symbol of the enemy’s security fell before the Iranian hero’s resolve, and the fortress finally came into Iranian hands. After his victory, Esfandiyar found his sisters and freed them from captivity.

Homay and Beh-Afarid left the fortress with the Iranian army, and Esfandiyar, having fulfilled his mission, prepared to return. The victory further strengthened his standing among Iran’s heroes: he had survived the Seven Labors and, through strategy and courage, opened a fortress whose conquest had seemed nearly impossible.

Yet his victorious return did not end Esfandiyar’s troubles. He hoped that after all these services, Goshtasp would keep his promise and give him the royal crown. Instead, his father once again placed a difficult task before him. Thus the victory at the Invulnerable Fortress became the beginning of a darker stage, one that would ultimately send Esfandiyar toward Zabul and his confrontation with Rustam.
30.originalVerse:
به رویین‌دژ آمد سوار دلیر
ز آهن دلش بود و رخساره شیر
ز هفت‌خوان گذشته، دل پرتوان
رسید از ره دور تا آن مکان
به تدبیر بگشاد راه حصار
نه تنها به شمشیر و تیغ و کارزار
چو در دژ درآمد خروشید جنگ
ز هر سو برآمد صدای خدنگ
سپاه ایران بر دشمن چیره شد
دل دژنشینان پر از بیم شد
همای و به‌آفرید از بند رست
دو شاهزاده از رنج و بند رست
چو پیروز شد آن یل نامدار
گمان برد کاید ز پس تخت و تاج
ولی گشتاسپ آورد فرمانی دگر
که شد راه اسفندیار پرخطر
ز پیروزی او نماندش مجال
که پیش آمدش داستانی محال

31.title: Part 31: Arjasp and the End of the Great War
31.prose:
After the opening of the Invulnerable Fortress, the conflict between Iran and Turan was still not over. Arjasp, unwilling to accept his repeated defeats, once again began thinking of gathering his forces and returning to the battlefield. Goshtasp also knew that the enemy still had the capacity to attack and that the Iranian army had to be prepared for another war.

Another battle broke out, and the two armies drew up against one another. In this battle, Esfandiyar was no longer merely a young man seeking fame; the experience of the Seven Labors and his victory at the Invulnerable Fortress had made him one of the Iranian army’s principal hopes. He fought beside the other heroes and carried the heavy burden of defending the country.

The fighting was fierce and costly. Many soldiers fell on the field, and every victory came with suffering and the loss of many lives. Nevertheless, Iran’s forces eventually defeated the Turanian army, and Arjasp was forced to retreat and flee. His defeat brought one of the greatest wars of this period to an end and, for a time, pushed the direct Turanian threat away from Iran’s borders.

Yet behind this victory, another matter remained unresolved. Esfandiyar expected Goshtasp, after years of service and difficult commands, to fulfill his promise of the kingship. Instead of reassuring his son, Goshtasp remained afraid of his power and popularity. Thus the end of the war did not mean the end of the conflict between father and son.

On one side, Esfandiyar was a victorious and beloved hero; on the other, he faced a father who repeatedly postponed his arrival on the throne to an uncertain future. This struggle would eventually lead Goshtasp to issue a new command: Esfandiyar was to be sent to Zabul, where Iran’s two great heroes, Esfandiyar and Rustam, would be set against one another. From here the story moves from war with an external enemy toward a tragedy within the royal and heroic family.
31.originalVerse:
ارجاسپ از کینه دلش پرخروش
به ایران کشید از سپاهش خروش
ز هر سو برآمد صدای سپاه
جهان شد پر از گرد میدان و راه
چو اسفندیار آمد از راه دور
شد از بیم او دل سپاه تور
بسی مرد جنگی به میدان فتاد
ز خون یلان دشت رنگی نهاد
سرانجام ایران به پیروزی رسید
و ارجاسپ از پیش ایشان رمید
ولی شاه با پسر آشتی نکرد
که بیم تخت از دل او دور نکرد
اسفندیار از پیِ تاج و تخت
همی جست از شاه پیمان و بخت
نمی‌دانست این راه پایان چه بود
که پیشش نبردی گران‌تر نمود

32.title: Part 32: Rustam and Esfandiyar — The Difficult Command
32.prose:
After years of war and heroism, Esfandiyar believed the time had come for Goshtasp to keep his promise and hand the royal crown to him. He had fought many battles for his father and his country, passed through the Seven Labors, and opened the Invulnerable Fortress; he expected now to receive the reward for all those services. But Goshtasp once again refused his request and placed a new mission before him.

The king’s command was that Esfandiyar go to Zabulistan and bring Rustam, Iran’s greatest hero, before him in chains. For Esfandiyar, this was no simple order. Rustam was not a hero who would easily submit, yet Esfandiyar could not ignore the command of his father and king. At the same time, there was no personal enmity between the two men, and both were among the great figures of Iran.

Esfandiyar traveled toward Zabulistan and delivered Goshtasp’s message to Rustam. Rustam knew his own standing and did not want, after a lifetime of service to Iran, to be taken to court like a prisoner. He said he was willing to go before the king, but that binding his hands and taking him by force was incompatible with a hero’s honor and the name of his family. Rustam tried to find a way to end the dispute through conversation.

Esfandiyar also knew that Rustam was a great and aged hero, and that fighting him could harm Iran. Nevertheless, he saw himself as responsible for obeying the king’s command. He said that if Rustam accepted the order, there would be no bloodshed or war; but if he refused, Esfandiyar would have no choice but to carry out his mission. Thus the two men became trapped between mutual respect and the duty each understood himself to bear.

Rustam again proposed that he go to Goshtasp without being bound and speak with him about the dispute. But Esfandiyar regarded the command as unequivocal and was unwilling to alter it. He said that if he disobeyed the king, he too would be accused of rebellion. Their words led nowhere, and the path of peace was closed.

At last, the confrontation between the two heroes began—not because one was an enemy of Iran and the other its defender, but because of a command that had come from the court. This is what makes their battle different from many other wars in the Shahnameh. Here tragedy begins where two great heroes could have been allies, but royal power and command place them on opposite sides of the field. The battle between Rustam and Esfandiyar now appears unavoidable.
32.originalVerse:
دو پهلوان آمدند از دو سوی
یکی در پی فرمان، یکی در پی خوی
یکی نامدار از نژاد کیان
یکی پهلوانِ کهن در جهان
اسفندیار گفت فرمان شاه
که رستم بیاید به درگاه شاه
رستم نپذرفت آن ننگ و بند
که آزاد مرد است و آزاده‌مند
بگفتا که من نزد شاه آیم به پای
ولی دست‌بسته نگردم به جای
چو راه سخن بسته شد در میان
برآمد ز هر دو سپاه، تیغ‌ران
نه کینه میان بود و نه دشمنی
که فرمان شد آغاز این روشنی
دو مرد بزرگ از دو سوی نبرد
که هر یک دلیر و به پیمان سپرد

33.title: Part 33: Rustam and Esfandiyar — The Battle of Two Heroes
33.prose:
پس از آنکه گفت‌وگو میان رستم و اسفندیار به نتیجه نرسید، دو پهلوان بزرگ ایران در برابر یکدیگر ایستادند. هر دو می‌دانستند که جنگ با دیگری آسان نیست و هر دو از پیامدهای این رویارویی بیم داشتند، اما فرمان شاه و آبروی پهلوانی راه بازگشت را تنگ کرده بود.

رستم با تجربهٔ سال‌های دراز و نیرویی که از نبردهای بی‌شمار به دست آورده بود، به میدان آمد. اسفندیار نیز جوان‌تر، نیرومند و برخوردار از زرهی بود که او را در برابر بیشتر سلاح‌ها رویین‌تن کرده بود. ضربه‌های رستم بر تن اسفندیار کارگر نمی‌افتاد و تیرها و نیزه‌ها راهی برای نفوذ در زره او پیدا نمی‌کردند.

نبرد طولانی شد و هیچ‌یک به آسانی پیروز نشد. رستم و رخش آسیب دیدند و پهلوان پیر دریافت که نیروی معمولی برای پایان دادن به این کار کافی نیست. او زخمی و خسته نزد زال رفت و از پدر خواست چاره‌ای بیندیشد. زال که خطر را جدی می‌دید، به یاد سیمرغ افتاد؛ همان مرغ افسانه‌ای که از کودکی در سرنوشت خاندان سام حضور داشت.

زال پر سیمرغ را به کار گرفت و سیمرغ فراخوانده شد. سیمرغ رستم و رخش را درمان کرد و پس از شنیدن ماجرای نبرد، راز شکست اسفندیار را آشکار ساخت. بدن اسفندیار در برابر سلاح‌ها آسیب‌ناپذیر بود، اما چشم‌های او از این مصونیت برخوردار نبودند. راه پیروزی، نه زور بیشتر، بلکه شناخت نقطهٔ ضعف پهلوان رویین‌تن بود.

رستم از اینکه باید چنین راهی را برگزیند خشنود نبود. اسفندیار دشمن شخصی او نبود و رستم می‌دانست که جوانی چون او قربانی فرمان پدر و بازی قدرت دربار شده است. با این حال، اگر خود را تسلیم می‌کرد، خاندان و آزادگی‌اش را از دست می‌داد و اگر می‌جنگید، احتمال کشته شدن یکی از دو پهلوان بزرگ ایران وجود داشت.

نبرد دوباره از سر گرفته شد. این بار رستم با دانشی که سیمرغ به او داده بود، تیر ویژه‌ای آماده کرد. لحظه‌ای فرا رسید که اسفندیار در تیررس قرار گرفت و رستم تیر را به سوی چشم او رها کرد. تیر به هدف نشست و اسفندیار، که تا آن لحظه شکست‌ناپذیر می‌نمود، بر زمین افتاد.

اسفندیار در واپسین لحظات دریافت که سرنوشت او بیش از آنکه ساختهٔ دشمنی با رستم باشد، نتیجهٔ فرمانی بود که از سوی پدرش آمده بود. او از رستم خواست مراقب بهمن، پسرش، باشد و آیندهٔ او را فراموش نکند. بدین ترتیب، پیروزی رستم رنگ شادی نداشت؛ زیرا با مرگ اسفندیار، ایران یکی از بزرگ‌ترین پهلوانان نسل تازه را از دست داد و رستم نیز بار دیگر قربانی تصمیم‌های شاهان شد.
33.originalVerse:
دو گرد از دو نسل آمدند به جنگ
دلیران به حیرت، سپاهان به تنگ
یکی پیر و آزموده در کارزار
یکی جوان و پرتوان و نامدار
زره بر تن اسفندیار استوار
نه شمشیر بر او داشت کارزار
نه تیر و نه نیزه بر او کار کرد
که رویین‌تن بود و دلیر و نبرد
رستم ز سیمرغ یاری گرفت
که از رنج این کار چاره گرفت
سیمرغ گفتا که راهی دگر
ببین در پس این نبرد پرخطر
تنش را ز آهن نشانده‌ست بخت
ولی چشم او نیست هم‌چون درخت
چو تیر از کمان رستم جدا شد
دل دشت از آن حادثه پرصدا شد
به چشم اسفندیار آن تیر نشست
و آن پهلوان نامدار از پای بست
به رستم سپرد آن زمان بهمنش
که باشد نگهبان و یاورِ تنش
پیروزی رستم پر از درد بود
که مرگ جوانی گران‌مایه بود

34.title: Part 34: The End of Esfandiyar and Bahman
34.prose:
پس از آنکه تیر رستم بر چشم اسفندیار نشست، پهلوان جوان دریافت که زخم او مرگبار است. پایان نبرد برای هیچ‌یک از دو پهلوان با شادی همراه نبود؛ زیرا رستم می‌دانست مردی را از میان برده که دشمن شخصی او نبود و اسفندیار نیز در واپسین لحظه‌ها دریافت که فرمان پدرش او را به چنین سرنوشتی کشانده است.

اسفندیار پیش از مرگ، رستم را سرزنش نکرد و از او خواست به یاد بهمن، پسر جوانش، باشد. او آیندهٔ فرزند خود را به پهلوان بزرگ ایران سپرد و خواست که بهمن راه و رسم پهلوانی را بیاموزد. این درخواست، تلخی نبرد را بیشتر کرد؛ زیرا دو خاندان که در میدان رویاروی هم قرار گرفته بودند، از راه بهمن دوباره به یکدیگر پیوند می‌خوردند.

رستم از مرگ اسفندیار سخت اندوهگین شد. او می‌دانست که اگر فرمان گشتاسپ نبود، این دو پهلوان می‌توانستند در کنار یکدیگر برای ایران بجنگند. از نگاه رستم، گشتاسپ برای حفظ تاج و جلوگیری از قدرت گرفتن پسرش، از فرمان شاهانه استفاده کرده و اسفندیار را به رویارویی با او فرستاده بود.

پس از مرگ اسفندیار، خشم و اندوه در خاندان گشتاسپ بالا گرفت. بهمن که هنوز جوان بود، در میان این کشمکش قرار داشت. رستم به عهد خود وفادار ماند و او را پذیرفت و پرورش داد. بدین ترتیب، بهمن مدتی در زابل و در کنار خاندان سام و زال با آیین پهلوانی آشنا شد و از تجربهٔ رستم بهره برد.

بهمن در وجود خود دو میراث مهم را حمل می‌کرد: از سوی پدر، جایگاه خاندان گشتاسپ و اسفندیار را و از سوی پیوندی که پس از مرگ پدر با رستم پیدا کرد، بخشی از سنت پهلوانی خاندان سام را. همین پیوند نشان می‌داد که حتی در دل دشمنی‌های خونین، شاهنامه راه‌هایی برای انتقال تجربه و میراث از نسلی به نسل دیگر می‌گشاید.

مرگ اسفندیار همچنین نشانهٔ پایان یک دوره بود. او آخرین پهلوان بزرگ نسل خود بود که با فرمان شاه به جنگ پهلوانی هم‌سنگ خویش رفت و در این راه جان باخت. رستم نیز پس از این حادثه بیش از پیش با بار سنگین گذشته و تصمیم‌های شاهان روبه‌رو شد.

از این پس، داستان به سوی نسل‌های تازه و دگرگونی قدرت پیش می‌رود. بهمن، که اکنون تحت حمایت رستم قرار گرفته بود، آینده‌ای متفاوت در پیش داشت و نام اسفندیار از راه او در تاریخ پهلوانی ایران باقی می‌ماند. میراث اسفندیار دیگر تنها خاطرهٔ یک پهلوان رویین‌تن نبود، بلکه در تربیت و سرنوشت فرزندش ادامه پیدا می‌کرد.

دل آن یل از رزم و پیکار رست

که آن پهلوان از میان رفته گشت
به رستم سپرد آن جوان بهمنش
که آموزدش راه و آیین و منش
بگفتا که این کودک یادگار من است
امید من از روزگار من است
رستم ز مرگش پر از درد شد

به یاد آمدش روزهای نبرد
که این کار جز رنج و ماتم نداشت

ز آیین مردی خبرها گرفت
نام اسفندیار از پسر زنده ماند
و آن داستان در جهان پاینده ماند

35.title: Part 35: Bahman and the Beginning of a New Generation
35.prose:
پس از مرگ اسفندیار، بهمن در میان دو میراث بزرگ رشد کرد. او فرزند پهلوانی بود که در نبردی تلخ به دست رستم کشته شده بود، اما همان رستم به عهد خود وفا کرد و بهمن را پذیرفت و آیین پهلوانی آموخت. از همین رو، کودکی و جوانی بهمن در سایهٔ خاطرهٔ دو پهلوان بزرگ سپری شد و او از هر دو خاندان چیزی برای آینده با خود برد.

بهمن در کنار رستم با رسم جنگاوری، وفاداری، سخن گفتن با بزرگان و شناخت دشواری‌های فرمانروایی آشنا شد. رستم برای او تنها پهلوانی نامدار نبود؛ بلکه آموزگاری بود که می‌توانست تجربهٔ نسل‌های پیشین را به جوانی منتقل کند. این رابطه، زخم میان دو خاندان را از راه یک نسل تازه تا اندازه‌ای به پیوندی انسانی تبدیل کرد.

با گذشت سال‌ها، بهمن به دربار بازگشت و جایگاه خود را در خاندان پدری شناخت. نام اسفندیار همچنان با خاطرهٔ جنگ با رستم همراه بود، اما بهمن مجبور نبود همهٔ دشمنی‌های گذشته را تکرار کند. او می‌توانست میراث پدر را با تجربه‌ای که از رستم گرفته بود درهم آمیزد و راهی تازه برای خود بسازد.

در این دوره، جهان پهلوانی نیز در حال دگرگونی بود. رستم و بسیاری از قهرمانان نسل پیشین دیگر در مرکز همهٔ رویدادها نبودند و قدرت سیاسی بیش از گذشته به خاندان‌های شاهی و نسل‌های تازه منتقل می‌شد. بهمن در چنین زمانی اهمیت پیدا کرد، زیرا میان گذشته و آینده ایستاده بود.

داستان بهمن نشان می‌دهد که میراث پهلوانی فقط از راه خون و نسب منتقل نمی‌شود. گاهی یک جوان می‌تواند از دو سوی یک دشمنی تاریخی تجربه بیاموزد و آن را به شکل دیگری ادامه دهد. بهمن از خاندان اسفندیار بود، اما سال‌هایی از تربیت او در کنار رستم گذشت؛ بنابراین گذشتهٔ متعارض ایران در شخصیت او به هم رسید.

با بازگشت بهمن به جایگاه سیاسی و درباری، مسیر داستان از تراژدی رستم و اسفندیار به دوره‌ای تازه نزدیک شد. دیگر مسئله تنها رویارویی دو پهلوان نبود؛ بلکه پرسش اصلی این بود که پس از پایان نسل بزرگ قهرمانان، چه کسانی بار فرمانروایی و دفاع از ایران را بر دوش خواهند گرفت.

بهمن سرانجام به پادشاهی رسید و نام او در شمار پادشاهان ایران قرار گرفت. دوران او آغاز مرحله‌ای تازه در روایت شاهنامه است؛ مرحله‌ای که در آن پیوند میان قدرت شاهی و میراث پهلوانی شکل دیگری پیدا می‌کند. خاطرهٔ رستم و اسفندیار همچنان باقی است، اما نسل تازه باید سرنوشت خود را رقم بزند.
35.originalVerse:
بهمن ز رستم هنرها گرفت
ز راه دلیران خبرها گرفت
ز یک سو غمِ نام اسفندیار
ز دیگر سو آیین مردان کار
دو خاندان در جان او گشته جمع
دو یاد کهن در دلش همچو شمع
چو سالی برآمد ز آن روزگار
به درگاه آمد جوان نامدار
نه کین پدر را به شمشیر جست
نه راه دلیران پیشین گسست
ز رستم شنید آنچه باید شنید
ز آیین مردی دل و جان کشید
چو هنگام تخت و کلاهش رسید
ز نسل پهلوانان دگرگونه دید
جهان پهلوانی دگرگون شده‌ست
که هر نسل را راه دیگر بود

36.title: Part 36: The Reign of Bahman
36.prose:
After Goshtasp, Bahman ascended the throne of Iran and took upon himself the legacy of his father and grandfather. In childhood and youth, he had lived with the memory of Esfandiyar and had learned the code of the hero from Rustam; his reign therefore stood between two great traditions: royal power and the culture of the champions.

At the beginning of his rule, Bahman sought to strengthen the authority of the government throughout the country. He organized the court and army and worked to secure the borders and consolidate the position of the Kayanian house. Yet the conflicts inherited from the previous generation were still alive, and the relationship between the court and the house of Zal was no longer as simple as before.

Rustam’s name remained bound to Iran’s greatest victories, but his death and then Esfandiyar’s showed that the age of the great heroes was changing. Bahman wanted to emphasize royal authority, and this brought him into tension with the powerful and independent houses of Sistan.

In accounts of this period, Bahman’s severity toward Zal’s family becomes one of the defining features of his reign. He had not forgotten his father’s death and saw a political distance between his own rule and Rustam’s legacy. This conflict was more than a personal enmity; it revealed a rivalry between two centers of power: the royal throne and the heroic house.

Bahman sought to consolidate his authority through armies and royal commands. Yet the Shahnameh shows that political power, however extensive, cannot easily endure without ties to the heroes and great men of the country. His reign therefore became entangled in the same question that had faced earlier generations: the relationship between king and hero.

After years of Bahman’s rule, succession entered a new stage. He had a daughter named Homay, and the story now turns toward her life and that of her son Darab. A new branch of the royal line begins to take shape, and the Shahnameh moves farther away from the heroic age of Sistan.

Bahman’s reign is, overall, a period of transition. On one side, Esfandiyar’s name and the Kayanian tradition remain central; on the other, a new generation of rulers and heroes is emerging. With the passing of Rustam and Esfandiyar’s generation, Iranian history enters a stage in which the throne and royal lineage assume a greater role.
36.originalVerse:
بهمن نشست از پسِ گشتاسپ شاه
به آیین تخت و کلاه و سپاه
ز اسفندیارش بمانده نشان
ز رستم به دل یادِ مردانِ جهان
به کشور همی جست فرمانروایی
به شمشیر و داد و بزرگواری
ولی کینهٔ دیرسال از میان
نرفت از دل آن شاهِ نام‌آوران
که تخت و سپاه و بزرگانِ کشور
به هر سو کشیدند راهی دگر
میان تخت شاه و خاندانِ زال
هنوز آشکارا بمانده‌ست جدال
چو هنگام جانشینی فراز آمد
داستان سوی همای بازآمد
ز همای آمد آن نسل نو
که تاریخ را داد رنگی دگر

37.title: Part 37: Homay Chehrazad and the Succession of a Woman
37.prose:
After Bahman, Homay Chehrazad took the throne of Iran and ruled for a number of years. Her place among the kings of the Shahnameh shows that the Iranian epic does not restrict authority and wisdom to men. Homay was a woman of judgment and power, able to govern the country while the memory of the great wars was still alive.

Homay belonged to the house of Goshtasp and Esfandiyar, so her succession continued that dynasty. Yet the atmosphere of the story changes in her time. The narrative is no longer centered only on the battles of heroes; the throne, succession, family secrets, and the future of the royal line become increasingly important.

Homay had a son named Darab. But the circumstances of the court and fear of disorder over the succession led her to conceal the child’s fate and separate him from herself. Darab was taken from his mother in childhood, and his life continued along an unknown path. This separation became one of the great secrets of this part of the story.

Years passed, and Darab grew up without fully knowing his true position. His fate gradually drew him toward the army and the court. Signs of his lineage and worth began to appear, until the story reached the point where his ancestry could no longer remain hidden.

Despite the difficult decision she had made about her son, Homay continued to bear the responsibility of kingship. In the Shahnameh, her rule represents a period in which preserving the country’s order and the continuity of the dynasty could require harsh and painful decisions.

Darab’s return to power was not merely a family matter. Once his lineage was revealed, the future of the crown changed again and a new generation of kings emerged. From here the story moves toward Darab and then another Bahman, the king who would later stand against Alexander’s power.

Homay Chehrazad therefore holds a special place in this chain of events: she is both king and mother, and her decision concerning Darab changes the course of succession. Her story shows that sometimes the fate of a dynasty is determined not on the battlefield, but in the silence of a palace and in the decision of a ruler.
37.originalVerse:
همای آمد و بر سر تخت نشست
به داد و خرد راه کشور ببست
زنی بود با فرّ و فرمان و رای
نگهبان ایران به هنگام پای
ز بهمن بمانده‌ست تخت و کلاه
همای آن نگه داشت با فرّ و جاه
ز داراب پنهان بماند آن نشان
که راز دلش بود با او نهان
کودک ز مادر جدا گشت و رفت
و در پردهٔ راز، سالی بگشت
چو سالی برآمد، جوانی پدید
که از چهره‌اش فرّ شاهی دمید
نشان‌های تبارش پدیدار شد
دلِ رازدار از نهان آگاه شد
ز مادر به فرزند راهی رسید
و تخت از پی آن دگرگونه دید
که گاه سرنوشت جهان و تاج
به یک راز گردد دگرگون‌ساز

38.title: Part 38: Darab and the Return of the Prince
38.prose:
Darab, the son of Homay, was finally recognized as the rightful heir after years away from the court. The signs of royal lineage were evident in him, and his ability and courage showed that he was prepared to rule. Once the secret of his ancestry was revealed, the course of succession changed again, and Darab took the throne of Iran.

At the beginning of his reign, Darab sought to preserve the country’s authority and keep its borders secure against its enemies. His period was marked by campaigns and political confrontations, and Iran’s relations with the lands to the west became increasingly important. From this point, the Shahnameh gradually enters a world in which Iran stands alongside Rome and more distant lands.

Darab fought his enemies to consolidate his power and did not retreat before rebellion or threat. In the epic narrative, his reign forms part of the chain of rulers who must preserve Iran’s inheritance for the next generation. Yet his fate also shows that no king can remain untouched by the great changes of his age.

In Darab’s life, lineage and succession remain crucial. He was the son of a mother who had herself sat upon the throne, and his return to power was the result of years in which the truth had been concealed. His kingship therefore continues the story begun with Homay: the secret of one family can change the future of an entire country.

Darab had a son named Dara, and after him the crown passed to another generation. Dara’s story brings Iran into an age in which contact with the Hellenic world and the name of Alexander move to the center of the narrative. Here the Shahnameh blends Iranian traditions about Alexander with historical and legendary material.

For Ferdowsi, Darab serves largely as a link: on one side he continues the Kayanian dynasty; on the other, he prepares the way for figures who carry the story of Iran from the earlier heroic world into a new age. After him, the central issue is no longer only the war between Iran and Turan, but Iran’s confrontation with western powers and the transformation of the world order.

The end of Darab’s reign begins the stage in which Dara and then Alexander enter the story. With this transition, the Shahnameh approaches one of its great turning points, where legend, history, and cultural memory stand together.
38.originalVerse:
داراب آمد ز دوری به تخت
دلش پر ز نیرو، سرش پر ز بخت
به ایران گرفت آن مهی را به داد
ز دشمن نترسید و کشور گشاد
ز مادر نشان داشت و از شاه نژاد
به تخت اندر آورد فرّ و داد
چو راز نهان آشکارا بگشت
سر تخت ایران دگرگونه گشت
به مرزهای دور آهنگ کرد
دلیرانه با دشمنان جنگ کرد
ز داراب ماند آن فرّ و نشان
که پیوند بود او میان دو جهان
ز تخم وی آمد یکی شاه نو
که تاریخ را برد سوی گفت‌وگو
ز دارا رسید آن زمان داستان
که اسکندر آمد به میدان جهان
جهان از پی آن دگرگون شد
حماسه به تاریخ هم‌چون شد

39.title: Part 39: Dara and the Confrontation with Alexander
39.prose:
Dara ascended the throne of Iran after Darab and inherited the dynasty in a difficult age. The world around Iran was changing, and the western powers were drawing closer to its borders. In the Shahnameh, the greatest threat came from Alexander, king of Macedon, who after his vast conquests advanced toward Iran.

At first, messages and negotiations passed between Dara and Alexander, but their dispute over power and territory finally led to war. Dara gathered a great army and sought to stand against the invaders. Iran possessed great numbers, yet on a battlefield numbers alone do not decide the outcome; the coordination of commanders and their loyalty matter as well.

The battles between the two sides were harsh and costly. Alexander advanced with an organized army and concentrated command, while Dara struggled to hold the Iranian forces together. Disagreements among some Iranian nobles and commanders made matters harder and damaged trust between the ruler and his army.

In Ferdowsi’s telling, Dara’s fate is linked not only to defeat in battle but also to the treachery and weakness of some of those close to him. He was wounded and fell away from the field. Alexander, seeking to end the war and claim Iran’s crown, eventually reached Dara.

In his final moments, Dara spoke of Iran’s future and the place of kingship. His death ended a dynasty that, in the Shahnameh, had begun with Kayumars and the first kings and had continued through many generations. With Dara’s fall, the Iranian kingship no longer continued in its former form, and Alexander entered a new stage of the story.

In the Shahnameh, Alexander is not merely a foreign conqueror; he is a figure to whom elements of Iranian culture and tradition are also attributed, and his story moves along the boundary between history and epic. After Dara’s death, Iran faces a new reality: a ruler who has come from outside must nevertheless find his place in the chain of kings within the Iranian story.

Dara’s end is therefore both the end of a dynasty and the beginning of a new chapter. From here the story moves away from the traditional wars of Iran and Turan toward Alexander’s journeys, conquests, and adventures, where the boundary between enemy, ruler, and hero becomes more complex.
39.originalVerse:
دارا به میدان سپه برکشید
ز هر سو هزاران سوار آفرید
به ایران همی گفت کاین روز جنگ
نگردد ز یاد جهان تا ابد زنگ
اسکندر آمد ز روم و سپاه
جهان شد پر از بانگ کوس و کلاه
دو کشور به یک رزم درهم شدند
دلیران بسیار بی‌سر شدند
ز هر سو یکی رای دیگر گرفت
دل شاه از آن کار برتر گرفت
چو دارا ز زخمی به بستر فتاد
دگرگونه شد تخت و تاج و نژاد
به نزدیک او رفت آن شهریار
که جست از پس این نبرد افتخار
دارا ز پایان ایران بگفت
ز بیداد و کین و ز کردار جفت
چو جان از تنش رفت، کیانی نماند
و تخت کهن شکل دیگر گرفت

40.title: Part 40: Alexander and the Legacy of Iran
40.prose:
After Dara’s defeat and the end of the Kayanian dynasty, Alexander entered Iran and regarded himself as heir to the fallen throne. Yet Ferdowsi’s account of him is not merely the story of a conqueror. Throughout his journeys, Alexander encounters scholars, sages, and many peoples, while also seeking to understand the world and the mysteries of life.

After establishing his power in Iran, Alexander set out for other lands. His army crossed beyond familiar frontiers, and each journey brought battle, wonder, and encounters with a new people. The world of the story expanded beyond Iran and Turan, and the geography of the epic widened with it.

On these journeys Alexander met many kings and rulers. At times he prevailed by the sword; at others he reached his goal through dialogue, wisdom, and an understanding of circumstances. This duality makes his character in the Shahnameh more complex than that of a simple conqueror.

Part of the narrative is devoted to the pursuit of knowledge and meetings with sages. Alexander seeks the experience of men who have spent years contemplating the world. He asks about death, life, fate, and the limits of power—questions from which even a victorious ruler cannot escape.

Alongside these quests, his campaigns toward the east and south continue. Distant lands, seas, mountains, and unfamiliar peoples enter the story, turning Alexander’s tale into part of a world-spanning epic. Iran is no longer merely a battlefield; it becomes the starting point of a journey that greatly widens the story’s horizon.

In his account of Alexander, Ferdowsi brings Iranian traditions together with the stories known about this ruler. Some of what we read carries the color of history, while other passages move through the world of legend and ancient tale. This mixture is one of the defining features of this part of the Shahnameh.

After many conquests, Alexander still seeks answers to his great questions. That search eventually carries the story toward the end of his life, where military power, distant journeys, and the desire for immortality confront the reality of death.
40.originalVerse:
چو اسکندر آمد ز راه دراز
به ایران رسید آن سرافراز
نه تنها به شمشیر کشور گشاد
که جست از خردمندان راهِ داد
جهان را همی دید و دانش گرفت
ز هر مرز و بوم اندر اندیشه رفت
ز کوه و ز دریا گذر کرد نیز
که بودش دل جوینده و تیز
گهی با سپه بود و گه با خرد
گهی راز گیتی ز دانا طلب کرد
ز هر شهری آوازه‌ای تازه یافت
ز هر مرزی اندیشه‌ای برگرفت
ولی هر چه گشت آن جهان پهن‌دشت
سرانجام دانست کاین راه گشت
نه تاج و نه شمشیر جاوید نیست
که پایان هر شاه را رفتن است

41.title: Part 41: Alexander in Egypt and His Journeys East
41.prose:
After securing his power in Iran, Alexander continued his great journeys and set out for distant lands. Egypt became an important destination, and from there his route turned eastward toward less familiar regions. The world of the story grows broader than ever, and Alexander encounters peoples, kings, and cultures that had previously played little part in the Iranian narrative.

In Egypt, Alexander is not concerned only with conquest. He encounters ancient monuments, rites, and bodies of knowledge, and is struck by the legacy of great civilizations. This part of the story shows that travel for him is not merely the movement of an army from one land to another, but also a search to understand the world.

Afterward he takes the eastern road. His army crosses hot and arid lands, mountains, and distant regions. Each place brings a new story and a new difficulty, and the ruler must choose among war, negotiation, and an understanding of local conditions. Sometimes victory comes by the sword; sometimes dialogue and judgment take the place of battle.

Throughout these journeys Alexander meets sages and learned men and asks questions about the mysteries of the world. The power he gained on the battlefield cannot answer all his questions. He wants to know what life means, how death overtakes human beings, and whether a ruler can overcome the passage of time.

In Ferdowsi’s narrative, this search becomes an important aspect of Alexander’s character. He is both conqueror and seeker, both intent on extending his realm and aware of the limits of human life. The farther he travels, the more clearly he encounters the truth that the world is far larger than the dominion of any single king.

The eastern lands are also filled with wonders and varied tales. New peoples, unfamiliar animals and landscapes, and stories about the limits of the world and distant countries shape this part of the narrative. Here the Shahnameh moves away from military history and toward an epic and legendary journey.

Yet however long a journey may be, it has an end. After his many conquests and encounters, Alexander approaches the final stage of his life. His fate will show that even a ruler who has brought a great part of the world under his command cannot pass beyond the law of time and death.
41.originalVerse:
ز مصر و ز هند و ز روم و ز چین
همی دید گیتی، برآورد کین
به هر مرز و بوم اندر افکند رای
که بیند چه دارد جهان از برای
ز هر جا یکی داستان تازه دید
ز هر دانشی بهره‌ای برگزید
گهی با سپه بود و گه با خرد
گهی راز گیتی ز دانا طلب کرد
ز کوه و ز دریا گذر کرد نیز
که بودش دل جوینده و تیز
جهان هرچه پیمود، فراخ‌تر شد
ولی عمر او نیز کوتاه‌تر شد
نه تخت بلندش ز مرگ ایمن است
نه لشکر رهاندش، نه تاج و نه گنج
سرانجام سفر سوی پایان گرفت
زمانه ره رفتنش را گرفت

42.title: Part 42: The Death of Alexander and the Return to the Iranian Story
42.prose: After years of campaigns and journeys through distant lands, Alexander finally fell ill. The ruler who had repeatedly emerged victorious from battle now faced an adversary that neither armies nor wealth nor the crown could defeat. In his final days he remembered the lands he had conquered, the cities he had seen, and the peoples he had met. After his death, his vast realm did not remain united; commanders and rulers divided its regions, and the political world changed. In the Shahnameh, this is more than the death of a conqueror: it closes the period Iran entered after Dara’s fall. Ferdowsi then briefly passes through the intervening ages and points toward the Parthians and, beyond them, the rise of Ardashir Babakan and the Sasanian dynasty. Alexander’s end confirms a recurring truth of the Shahnameh: power and world conquest do not last; what remains is the name, conduct, and memory a ruler leaves behind.
42.originalVerse:
جهانگیر چون دید پایان کار
نهان شد ز تخت و ز تاج و نگار
نه گنجش بماند و نه لشکر به جای
که مرگ است فرجام هر تخت و رای
ز بیماری افتاد آن شهریار
که بسیار دیده بود روزگار
به یاد آمدش راه‌های دراز
ز مصر و ز هند و ز روم و ز راز
چه سود آن همه کشور و تاج و گنج
چو آمد سرانجام مرگ و درنگ
پس از او جهان گشت پر از پادشاه
هر آن سو یکی برکشیدند کلاه
بماند از وی آوازه‌ای در جهان
ولی تخت او رفت از آن میان
ز پس آن زمان داستانی دگر
رسید از ره تاریخ سوی ایران‌زمین

43.title: Part 43: The Parthians — A Bridge Between Two Ages
43.prose: After Alexander’s death, Iran entered a period that Ferdowsi treats briefly. The Parthians stand between Alexander’s world and the rise of the Sasanians. Although historically long and important, this age receives far less narrative space than the Kayanian and Sasanian periods. Iran was divided among different powers, yet the idea of Iran and the memory of ancient kings remained alive. In this political landscape the Sasanian family gained power in Fars, and Ardashir Babakan gradually expanded his influence. His aim was not a local kingdom but the reunification of Iran under one authority. With Ardashir, the Shahnameh becomes more cohesive again, following kings, wars, government, and foreign enemies in greater detail. The Parthian age therefore serves as a bridge from the post-Alexander world to Sasanian Iran.
43.originalVerse:
ز اشکانیان ماند نامی به جای
میان دو زمان و دو تخت و کلاه
نه داستانشان چون کیان پر ز راز
که آمد پس از اسکندر این روزگار
جهان بود پراکنده و تخت‌ها جدا
ولی نام ایران نماند از صدا
ز هر گوشه فرمانروایی پدید
و هر خاندان راه خویش آفرید
چو ساسان برآمد به فرّ و نژاد
ز خاندان او مردی آمد به داد
اردشیر آمد از تخم شاه
دگر بار برخاست فرّ و سپاه
به گردآوری کشور همت گماشت
ز ویرانیِ روزگارش بکاست
میان دو زمان این سخن یادگار
که از پس پراکندگی آمد قرار

44.title: Part 44: Ardashir Babakan and the Rise of the Sasanian Empire
44.prose: Ardashir Babakan rose to power when Iran was divided among rival rulers and families after a long period of political fragmentation. From the house of Sasan, he understood that ruling all Iran required confronting competing powers. He expanded his influence and fought rulers unwilling to surrender their authority. His wars were not merely territorial campaigns: his aim was to restore a unified political order. His decisive confrontation with Ardavan, the last Parthian king, marked the end of an era. After victory, Ardashir organized the country, army, and government, seeking the support of the great nobles and strengthening the foundations of the new state. Iranian rites and traditions also gained greater prominence. In the Shahnameh, Ardashir becomes a symbol of Iranian authority returning after disorder. He is therefore not only founder of a dynasty, but a sign of political unity restored to Iran.
44.originalVerse:
اردشیر آمد ز راه نبرد
به ایران یکی پادشاهی سپرد
ز اردوان تاج شاهی گرفت
ز هر گوشه‌ای راه و پناهی گرفت
ز پراکندگی کشورش را برآورد
به نیروی شمشیر و تدبیر و مرد
چو کشور یکی شد به فرمان او
فزون گشت فرّ و سامان او
سپاه و دربار را داد نظم
که بی‌نظم کشور نبیند جز رزم
ز آیین کهن پاسداری نمود
دل مردمان را به امید فزود
به ساسانیان داد بنیاد و نام
که ماند از پس او در ایران دوام
پس از روزگارِ پرآشوب و جنگ
برآورد تختی به آیین و سنگ

45.title: Part 45: Shapur and the Consolidation of the Empire
45.prose:
After Ardashir Babakan, Shapur ascended the Sasanian throne and continued his father's legacy. The newly founded Sasanian state still had to establish its authority against foreign enemies and rival rulers. Shapur quickly showed that he was not merely heir to the crown, but capable of building and extending power in his own right.

One of his principal arenas of conflict was Rome. Iran and Rome had long competed over frontier territories and political influence. Shapur led his armies through difficult wars and, in several battles, demonstrated Iran's power to its adversary. These wars strengthened the standing of the Sasanians against one of the greatest powers of the ancient world.

In Ferdowsi's account, Shapur's glory is not limited to victory in battle. He also attended to the organization and prosperity of the country. Building cities, strengthening roads, and securing the foundations of government were among his responsibilities, showing that military power could not endure without internal order.

Shapur also carried Ardashir's legacy to the next generation. Under him, the Sasanian government grew from a newly founded dynasty into a powerful empire. The name of the Sasanians was now known beyond Iran and associated with strength and authority in neighboring lands.

The wars with Rome also carried heavy costs. Large armies, broad frontiers, and prolonged rivalry affected rulers and ordinary people alike. Yet Shapur maintained the advantage through much of the struggle and consolidated Iran's position.

His reign marks an important point in the Shahnameh because Sasanian Iran moves from foundation into power and expansion. After him the empire would face new kings and crises, but the foundations laid by Ardashir and strengthened by Shapur would endure for a long time.

Shapur's name in this account is joined to two ideas: war to preserve and extend Iran's frontiers, and prosperity to strengthen the country from within. Together they complete his image as one of the important kings of the early Sasanian age.
45.originalVerse:
شاپور بر تخت پدر برنشست
به آیین شاهی کمر را ببست
به روم اندر آوای لشکر شکست
ز مرزها بگذشت آواز او
فزون گشت در جهان ساز او
ز هر سو سپاهی به میدان کشید
دل دشمن از نام او برمید
به جنگ و به آباد کردن دیار
نهاد از خود آن شاه یادگار
ز شهری به شهری دگر ساخت راه
که پاینده ماند آن شکوه و سپاه
چو ایران به نیروی او استوار
شد آوازه‌اش در جهان ماندگار
نه تنها به شمشیر جست آن شکوه
که آباد کرد کشور از راه و کوه

46.title: Part 46: Bahram Gur and the Royal Hunt
46.prose:
Bahram Gur is one of the best-known Sasanian kings in the Shahnameh, a ruler whose name is especially associated with hunting, above all the hunting of onagers. In his stories, the plain and wilderness are not merely the setting for royal amusement; they are also arenas in which his ability, courage, and kingship are tested.

From childhood and youth, Bahram was devoted to riding and hunting. Horsemanship, archery, and confronting wild animals formed part of his royal education. These skills later became signs of his character, while the epithet Gur became associated with his famous pursuit of the wild ass.

Yet in Ferdowsi's telling, Bahram is not merely a powerful hunter. A king must possess justice and generosity alongside strength and courage. His stories therefore move repeatedly between pleasure and responsibility, revelry and warfare, and the king's personal desires and his duty to the realm.

Bahram also proves himself against claimants to the crown and against enemies. For him, kingship means more than sitting upon a throne and enjoying its splendor; he must demonstrate his worth in politics and war and preserve the security of the land.

His famous hunts sometimes carry an ethical lesson as well. The hunter must know measure and timing, and the king must understand that every pleasure stands alongside a greater responsibility. Thus Bahram's courage acquires meaning only together with wisdom and moderation.

His reign belongs to a stage of the Shahnameh in which Sasanian history is woven together with heroic tales and moral stories. Bahram has a more story-like character than many other kings, and his life provides material for numerous accounts of travel, hunting, feasting, and tests of kingship.

In Iranian literary memory, Bahram Gur ultimately remained the image of a king riding across the plain with bow in hand in pursuit of the onager. Yet his importance in the Shahnameh goes beyond hunting: he represents a ruler who must balance martial strength, the pleasures of life, and the responsibilities of kingship.
46.originalVerse:
بهرام گور آن شاه شکارافکن
به دشت اندر آمد چو شیر ژیان
به گور و به نخجیر دل بسته بود
ولی داد را نیز پیوسته بود
کمان برکشید و به میدان شتافت
ز هر سو که گور آمد او را شتافت
به زین اندرون تیز و گردان‌سوار
چو آذرخش آمد به دشت شکار
ز هر سو که آمد به میدان شکار
بماند از وی آوازهٔ شهریار
ولی شاه را داد باید به پیش
که بی‌داد گردد جهان کم ز خویش
بزم و شکار ارچه خوش بود و نیک
خرد باید اندر میان، اندکی
چو شاه از ره داد یک دم نگشت
نامش به نیکی در جهان ماند گشت

47.title: Part 47: Kavadh and the Beginning of a New Age
47.prose:
Kavadh came to the Sasanian throne when the country faced internal divisions, rivalry among great families, and pressure from foreign enemies. His reign was unsettled from the beginning, and power at court was divided among competing groups.

During this period the Mazdakite movement spread in Iran. Mazdak and his followers spoke of social justice, narrowing the gap between the wealthy and the poor, and changing the existing order. These ideas appealed to some people and gained influence among sections of society.

Kavadh supported the movement for a time, and this association altered the balance of power at court. Opposing nobles and priests feared the new influence of the Mazdakites and eventually removed Kavadh from the throne. But this was not the end of his story: the deposed king managed to return to power.

His restoration came with new experience. He had learned that government could not endure without stable political and military structures. During his second reign, therefore, he devoted greater attention to organizing the country and strengthening the foundations of imperial authority.

At the same time Iran faced foreign enemies, and its eastern and western frontiers required constant attention. Kavadh ruled between two necessities: calming internal conflict and defending the borders of a country that remained one of the great powers of the world.

From this period, the historical face of Sasanian Iran becomes more complex. The king is no longer only a hero on the battlefield; politics, economics, social classes, and competing ideas also directly shape the fate of the country. Kavadh stands at the center of these changes.

His reign prepared the way for his son, Khosrow Anushirvan, a king known in the Shahnameh for justice, reform, and authority. Kavadh's story therefore forms a link between the Sasanians' internal crises and the period of their greatest political organization.
47.originalVerse:
قباد آمد و روزگارش شگفت
ز هر سو سخن‌های تازه گرفت
ز دربار برخاست غوغای رای
که هر کس همی جست راه و جای
سخن از تهی‌دست و توانگر فتاد
که هر کس به اندازهٔ خویش داد
ز مزدک سخن در جهان اوفتاد
که از داد و آیین نو کرد یاد
قباد از پی آن سخن راه جست
ولی کار کشور به دشواری است
ز تختش برآوردند از بیم و کین
دگر بار بنشست بر تخت خویش
به تدبیر و اندیشه آراست کار
سپاه و درفش و دربار را
ز دشمن نگه داشت مرز و کنار
چو بازآمد آن شاه بر تخت خویش
دگرگونه شد روزگار و کیش
از آن پس پدید آمد آن راه نو
که شد زمینه‌ساز شهریار نکو

48.title: Part 48: Khosrow Anushirvan and Justice
48.prose:
Anushirvan, son of Kavadh, succeeded his father on the Sasanian throne and began one of the most important periods of the dynasty. In Ferdowsi's account, his name is above all associated with justice, the ordering of the country, and the use of wisdom. His reign embodies the idea that a king's glory depends on more than victory in war.

To strengthen the government, Anushirvan organized the administration and army. Taxation, roads, the security of cities, and defense of the frontiers had to be placed within a clear order. He understood that a great empire could not endure without a strong administrative apparatus.

Beside him stood Bozorgmehr, the renowned minister and sage. Many stories of his conversations with the king and his wise answers survived in Iranian tradition. In this narrative, Bozorgmehr represents knowledge that tempers royal power and helps weigh difficult decisions.

Anushirvan also showed concern for justice among the people. In the stories surrounding him, the king must know the condition of farmers and ordinary people and must not allow taxes and court demands to ruin their lives. Justice here is not merely a personal virtue; it is a foundation of stable rule.

He was also a powerful ruler in foreign affairs, warring and making treaties with Iran's enemies, especially the great powers around it. Under him the Sasanian army was highly organized and powerful, and Iran retained its position among the great powers of the world.

Yet the Shahnameh's image of Anushirvan is not simply that of a victorious ruler. His stories repeatedly place the king before ethical questions: Is wealth without justice worthwhile? Can rule endure without listening to the wise? Is the security of a country possible without the people's consent?

For this reason Anushirvan's name became linked in Iranian memory with justice. His reign is one of the highest points of the Shahnameh's Sasanian narrative, after which the story moves toward kings who either continue some part of its splendor or confront its decline.
48.originalVerse:
چو نوشیروان بر سر تخت شد
جهان از خردمندی او نیک شد
به داد و دهش نام او گشت بلند
ز بیداد بر بست راه گزند
بزرگمهر را خواند نزدیک خویش
که جست از خرد راه و آیین خویش
به داد و به تدبیر کشور بداشت
ز هر کار نادر سخن‌ها نگاشت
به حال ضعیفان نظر داشت شاه
نمی‌خواست ویران شود دادخواه
سپاه و دیوان به سامان کشید
ز مرز و ز بوم ایران نگه دید
اگر شهریاری ز داد اوفتد
دل مردمان از وی آزاد شد
چنین گفت و کرد آن خردمند شاه
که پاینده ماند از عدالت کلاه
ز دانش گرفت آنچه بایست یاد
که نامش بماند به گیتی به داد

49.title: Part 49: Bozorgmehr and Wisdom at Anushirvan’s Court
49.prose:
Bozorgmehr is one of the Shahnameh's most distinguished figures of wisdom and statecraft. He holds a special place at Anushirvan's court, and his role is not limited to serving as a minister or managing affairs; he represents a form of knowledge capable of keeping royal power from haste and tyranny.

Anushirvan turns to Bozorgmehr on many difficult decisions. Before answering, the wise minister considers the different sides of a matter and sometimes clarifies a complex problem with a few words. Through these exchanges, the dialogue between king and minister becomes an important part of the Sasanian narrative.

In the stories attributed to Bozorgmehr, wisdom means more than book learning. Understanding people, recognizing the right moment, restraining anger and greed, and seeing the consequences of a decision are all forms of wisdom. A good minister is one who does not hide the truth even from power.

Bozorgmehr remains calm before difficult questions. He reminds the king that rule without justice and prudence will sooner or later lose its foundations. In this vision, a sword may defeat an enemy, but only order and wisdom can keep a country secure.

He also represents an old Iranian tradition in which king and sage stand beside one another. The king possesses power and the sage possesses discernment; both succeed when each completes the other and power does not become separated from wisdom.

Bozorgmehr's tales are sometimes told through questions and answers, riddles, and counsel. This structure allows the story to move beyond court affairs and speak about death, fortune, friendship, knowledge, wealth, and the proper way to treat other human beings.

For this reason, Bozorgmehr in the Shahnameh is more than a historical minister. He is a literary image of the wise counselor, whose value becomes clear in a crisis and who reminds the king that the greatest power is the ability to see the truth and accept it.
49.originalVerse:
بزرگمهر آن مرد روشن‌روان
به شاه اندر آموخت آیین جان
ز هر پرسش او پاسخی داشت راست
دل شاه از اندیشه‌ها کرد کاست
خرد را به تخت اندرون راه داد
که بی‌دانشی را نماندش نهاد
چو شاه از سر خشم گفتی سخن
وزیرش بیاراست گفتار خویش
نه با تندی و کین، که با رای و داد
دل شاه را سوی آرام داد
که تخت استوار از خرد می‌بود
نه از زور و شمشیر و لشکر فزود
ز دانش سخن گفت و از کار جهان
ز نیکی، ز بدی، ز سود و زیان
هر آن کو خرد را نگه داشت راست
در سختی او را پناهی بجاست
بزرگمهر از درگاه شاه
به دانش بیفزود فرّ و کلاه

50.title: Part 50: Khosrow Parviz and the Splendor of the Court
50.prose:
Khosrow Parviz is one of the best-known kings of the later Sasanian period in the Shahnameh. With his accession, the image of the court reaches a peak of splendor and luxury. Vast treasures, great palaces, swift horses, and continual celebrations evoke the picture of a powerful and wealthy empire.

In Khosrow's time, the war with Rome continues. Iranian armies advance in parts of the conflict, and the empire expands for a time. These victories increase the king's glory and spread his name across the surrounding lands.

But great power does not always mean peace. As the court grows larger, so does the number of claimants and influential figures. Behind the outward splendor, internal rivalries and the government's dependence on the person of the king create fragile foundations.

In the stories of this period, Khosrow Parviz is deeply attached to the wealth and beauty of his court. His treasures are signs of power, but Ferdowsi places an ethical question behind the magnificent image: can the accumulation of gold and the building of palaces truly change the fate of a person or a country?

In later years, the long wars impose heavy costs on both Iran and Rome. The two great powers become exhausted, and lands suffer from the consequences of conflict. The military splendor that first signaled strength gradually becomes a heavy burden upon government.

Khosrow's fate is tied to this contradiction. A king who has reached the height of power and wealth eventually proves unable to withstand political disorder and internal enemies. His deposition and death signal the beginning of the rapid collapse of Sasanian order.

Thus the story of Khosrow Parviz in the Shahnameh is more than the account of a wealthy king. He embodies rise and decline: a power that reaches its highest point and then begins to fall through war, luxury, and political conflict. After him, short-lived kings follow one another, and Iran approaches the final stage before the Arab conquest.
50.originalVerse:
خسرو برنشست و جهان گشت رام
ز گنجش پر از گوهر و سیم و جام
ز هر سو درِ گنج‌ها باز کرد
به شادی درِ بزم و آواز کرد
به روم اندرون بانگ لشکر فکند
ز هر مرز آواز پیروزی افکند
ز کاخ و ز ایوان برافراخت تخت
که دیدار او بود با گنج و بخت
ولی جنگ بسیار و سال دراز
بفرسود لشکر، شد آن کار باز
چو افزون شد آن شکوه و سپاه
دل شاه غافل شد از رنج راه
هر آن تاج کز زر برآراستند
ز گردون سرانجام برداشتند
به گیتی نماند آن شکوه بلند
که مرگ است پایان هر سود و گزند
چو خسرو ز تخت اندر آمد فرود
زمانه دگر کرد آیین و بود

51.title: Part 51: Khosrow and Shirin — Love and Kingship
51.prose:
The story of Khosrow and Shirin is shorter in the Shahnameh than in later literary retellings, yet even this brief account offers an important image of Khosrow Parviz's personal and political life. Shirin is not merely a silent beloved; she is a woman of will and character whose position affects the king's decisions.

Khosrow stands between personal attachment and the responsibilities of kingship. His position does not allow private life to remain separate from politics. Any relationship at court can affect succession, the king's authority, and his relations with the great nobles.

Shirin, too, appears as an independent figure in the face of this complicated world. She does not rely solely on Khosrow's power to obtain what she wants, and in the stories concerning the two, dialogue and conflict between the characters are important.

In later Iranian literary tradition, this love story expanded greatly, and other poets turned it into a long independent narrative. In the Shahnameh, however, it remains within the framework of Khosrow Parviz's life and serves chiefly as part of the portrait of a powerful but conflicted king.

Alongside love, court rivalry is also present. The king must balance personal desire, the interests of government, and pressure from those around him. This makes the relationship between Khosrow and Shirin not merely a love story, but also part of a king's political life.

In Iranian tradition, Shirin gradually became a symbol of love joined with dignity and self-respect. Her character shows that a woman in a courtly story is not merely an object of a king's desire; she can participate in decisions, dialogue, and political destiny.

Together with Khosrow Parviz's splendor and wars, the story of Khosrow and Shirin reveals a more human side of the king. The ruler who commands in politics must also confront choice, attachment, and the consequences of his decisions in private life; this duality is one of the lasting features of his story.
51.originalVerse:
خسرو ز شیرین سخن‌ها شنید
ز مهرش دل از خویشتن برکشید
ولی تخت شاهی و آیین داد
میان دل و کشورش سد نهاد
نه دل را توانست از مهر کند
نه کشور توانست یکسر نهاد
ز شیرین دلش سوی آرام رفت
ولی راه دربار دشوار یافت
چو عشق و سیاست به هم درگرفت
دل شاه از این هر دو راهی گرفت
زنی بود شیرین دل‌آگاه و پاک
که نلرزید از بیم تخت و هلاک
به گفتار و رای خویش استوار
نمود از زنان چهره‌ای ماندگار
که عشق ارچه شیرین بود در جهان
نباید ز خرد دور ماند ناگهان
از این داستان ماند در یادگار
پیوند دل با شکوه شهریار

52.title: Part 52: Bahram Chobin and the Revolt Against the King
52.prose:
Bahram Chobin is one of the most renowned Iranian commanders of the late Sasanian period. His reputation on the battlefield became so great that soldiers and many nobles regarded his courage and ability as equal to the king's power. That fame eventually brought him into conflict with the Sasanian throne.

At first, the disagreement between Bahram and Hormozd, and later Khosrow Parviz, arose from political and military questions. Bahram believed he deserved greater respect and reward, and he felt slighted by the king's commands. The conflict deepened when defeats and court decisions destroyed trust between commander and king.

Bahram rebelled, and part of the army joined him. The revolt was no longer a personal dispute; it placed the country between two powers: a king claiming the right to rule and a commander controlling a large part of the military force.

Khosrow Parviz was forced to leave Iran during the crisis. He sought help from Rome in order to regain power, and Iran's fate became tied to the rivalry between two rulers and two political forces. Civil war threatened to weaken the foundations of the empire even further.

In the end, forces loyal to Khosrow defeated Bahram. Bahram fled east, and the immediate crisis ended, but his name remained in Iranian history and literature as that of a great commander. His defeat did not diminish his military ability or courage.

The story of Bahram Chobin is one of the clearest examples of the conflict between merit and legitimacy. On one side stands a commander of extraordinary ability and popularity; on the other stands a king who represents the legitimacy of the throne. The Shahnameh presents this tension as a political tragedy.

The end of Bahram's revolt shows that military power alone is not enough to build a kingdom. A commander who can lead a great army may, when opposed to political order and royal legitimacy, become a source of disorder himself. His story is one of the Shahnameh's strongest warnings about the danger of a rupture between crown and army.
52.originalVerse:
بهرام آن سردار گردن‌فراز
برآمد ز فرمان و شد سرفراز
به میدان جنگش نبود هم نبرد
ز شمشیر او دشمنان گشت زرد
سپاه از پی او به میدان دوید
ز تخت شاهی سخن‌ها شنید
چو کین میان شاه و سردار خاست
دل کشور از بیم و آشوب کاست
خسرو ز ایران برون رفت خوار
طلب کرد یاری ز روم آن دیار
ز هر سو برآمد خروش سپاه
دو لشکر کشیدند بر یک راه
سرانجام بخت از بهرام برگشت
دل شورشی را زمانه ز کشت
بهرام سوی شرق روی آورد
ولی نام او در جهان ماند و مرد
که مردان میدان اگر سرکشند
ز تاج و ز کشور جدا کی شوند
چنین است پیوند شمشیر و تاج
که بی‌داد و تدبیر گردد علاج

53.title: Part 53: Khosrow and Farhad — The Heroic Tale of Love
53.prose:
Farhad, in the stories connected with Khosrow and Shirin, represents a world different from the court. He is neither king nor commander, but an artist and mountain-cutter whose love for Shirin is expressed not through power or treasure, but through labor and suffering.

Farhad falls in love with Shirin, and this devotion places him in opposition to Khosrow. Unable to tolerate such a sincere and admired rival, Khosrow sets him an almost impossible task: a great mountain must be cut through to open a path toward what he desires.

Instead of fearing the task, Farhad takes up his pick and strikes into the mountain. Here the mountain becomes a symbol of the obstacle between a human being and what he desires. Every blow of the pick becomes a sign of the lover's endurance and determination.

In later literary tradition, Farhad's story expanded greatly and became one of the best-known examples of tragic love in Persian literature. In the structure of the Shahnameh, however, it remains on the edge of the Khosrow and Shirin story and chiefly reveals another aspect of Khosrow's character and rivalry.

Farhad's love places him before the king's power. He possesses nothing but the sincerity of his feeling and the strength of his arms, while Khosrow has the crown, army, and court. This inequality turns the story from a love rivalry into a story about power as well.

Eventually false news about Shirin reaches Farhad, and his hope collapses. The bitter ending shows that in the epic and courtly world, a person does not always face only stone and mountains; sometimes deceit can be the hardest obstacle.

In Iranian literary memory, Farhad became a symbol of self-sacrificing love. If Khosrow represents royal power and splendor, Farhad represents the person without crown or throne who, through suffering and perseverance, tries to remain faithful to an ideal.
53.originalVerse:
فرهاد از پی مهر شیرین شتافت
ز کوه گران راهی دیگر شکافت
به تیشه دل خویش بر سنگ زد
ز عشقش جهان را به یک رنگ زد
نه تاجی به سر داشت و نه گنج و تخت
دلش بود سرمایه، امیدش بخت
چو فرمان رسید از در شهریار
که این کوه بشکاف و برکن غبار
به نیروی عشقش به کار آمد او
نه از رنج ترسید و نه از گفت‌وگو
ز هر ضربهٔ تیشه بانگش بلند
که عشق است کوه و اراده گزند
ولی قدرت شاه و نیرنگ راه
نهاد از میان عاشقان سد و چاه
خبر تلخ آمد ز شیرین به گوش
دل مرد عاشق پر از درد و جوش
چو امید از او گشت یکباره دور
فرو ریخت آن کوه و آن آرزوی نور

54.title: Part 54: The End of Khosrow Parviz
54.prose:
Khosrow Parviz, long known for the splendor of his court, immense wealth, and military victories, faced a very different image of kingship at the end of his reign. Long wars, internal hostility, and pressure from the great nobles had weakened the foundations of his power.

The war with Rome, which had first offered an opportunity to expand power, became a war of exhaustion. Armies remained engaged for years, and the cost of war weighed heavily upon the country. The great victories of the past could no longer conceal the government's internal weaknesses.

At the same time, Khosrow's opponents gained greater influence at court. The king whose commands had once been obeyed without question now faced rebellion and disobedience. Eventually he was removed from the throne, opening the way for rapid changes of rule.

After his deposition, Khosrow was no longer the powerful king of earlier years. The man who had once ruled vast territories was now trapped by decisions made by those who had risen within the power structure around him. His life ended under bitter and violent circumstances.

The death of Khosrow Parviz was not merely the end of a king's life; it also signaled the beginning of the political collapse of the Sasanians. After him, kings succeeded one another rapidly, many ruling only briefly. The stability built under Ardashir and Anushirvan was now disappearing quickly.

In this section, the Shahnameh moves more rapidly from one king's name to another. That speed itself signals disorder: there is no longer time to build a stable reign, and the crown passes among claimants and princes.

The fate of Khosrow Parviz, set beside the splendor of his earlier years, is one of the clearest examples in the Shahnameh of the instability of power. The throne built high eventually fell, and treasure and armies could not save its owner from destiny. From here the story approaches the final years of the Sasanian Empire.

55.title: Part 55: The Short-Lived Kings and the Turmoil of Iran
55.prose:
After the death of Khosrow Parviz, the Sasanian Empire entered one of the most turbulent periods of its history. The throne, once a symbol of authority and stability, passed in a short time among different princes and claimants. Each king came to power only to face another crisis before he could establish his rule.

The problem was not simply the brevity of the reigns. The court had become an arena of rivalry among powerful families and factions, each seeking to place its own candidate on the throne. Disputes over succession weakened trust between the great nobles and the government.

The army was also affected by this disorder. An army that had once been able to stand against Rome and other enemies was now drawn into internal rivalries. Commanders and troops no longer always received orders from a single center, and this weakened the country's ability to defend itself.

Beyond the borders, enemies found greater opportunity. Iran, exhausted by long wars with Rome, now had to face internal problems and external pressure at the same time. A country once known for central order and power was gradually losing its ability to respond quickly.

The Shahnameh deliberately moves through this period at speed. Ferdowsi names one king after another, and the disappearance of time for long narratives itself becomes an image of instability. When the throne acquires a new owner every day, history moves like a troubled river.

Yet even within this disorder, there are attempts to restore order. Nobles, soldiers, and powerful families try to find a way through the crisis and continue the government. But the foundations of the empire have been damaged so deeply that rebuilding authority is no longer easy.

The short-lived kings are therefore more than a list of names. They mark a stage in which the structure of a great empire has been worn down from within. After them, the narrative reaches the last Sasanian kings and finally Yazdegerd III, the final ruler of the dynasty and the last scene before a great transformation in Iranian history.

56.title: Part 56: Yazdegerd III and the Beginning of the End of the Sasanians
56.prose:
Yazdegerd III was the last Sasanian king, a young ruler who took the crown at an extraordinarily difficult moment. Before he reached the throne, the country had endured years of court conflict, rapid changes of kings, and exhausting wars. Yazdegerd inherited a great empire that was weary within and threatened from without.

In those same years, the Arab armies entered Sasanian territory from the west. The encounter between the two powers led to a series of great battles and changed the course of Iranian history. Yazdegerd tried to gather forces and defend the country, but the unified apparatus of the age of Anushirvan and Shapur no longer existed.

The battles of al-Qadisiyyah and then Nahavand dealt severe blows to Sasanian power. Defeat in these fields meant more than the loss of an army: the roads to major cities and provinces were opened to the invading forces, and the political center of the empire came increasingly under threat.

Yazdegerd moved from one city to another and tried to organize resistance. But as time passed, his resources and support diminished. Local nobles and provincial rulers no longer stood together around a single center as they once had, and this fragmentation weakened Iran's defenses.

With the fall of the capital and the loss of important parts of the country, Yazdegerd moved east. His journey was no longer that of a victorious king, but an effort to find new strength and preserve the last signs of kingship. At this stage, the Shahnameh moves from the splendor of the court to the tragic fate of a king whose crown can no longer save his country.

Yazdegerd was eventually killed at Merv, and with his death the Sasanian dynasty ended. Yet the end of a dynasty did not mean the end of Iran. Its language, culture, stories, and memory of earlier kings survived and continued in new forms.

The story of Yazdegerd III matters in the Shahnameh because it marks the end of a political world. From Kayumars to the Sasanians, the narrative has repeatedly spoken of kings rising and falling; now one historical age comes to an end and its inheritance passes to later generations.

57.title: Part 57: The Battle of al-Qadisiyyah and the Collapse of the Iranian Army
57.prose:
The Battle of al-Qadisiyyah was one of the most important confrontations of the final Sasanian period. The Iranian army faced the Arab forces, and the outcome changed the course of the region's history. Iran had already been weakened by internal crises and long wars, and now it had to confront a new and highly mobile power.

The Iranian army entered the field with large numbers of warriors and commanders. Rustam Farrokhzad was one of the leading figures of the battle and carried a heavy responsibility. Yet internal divisions, the exhaustion of the army, and difficult political circumstances had reduced Iran's defensive strength compared with earlier periods.

The battle was hard and prolonged, and both sides suffered heavy losses. In the epic narrative, the battlefield is not merely the scene of two armies confronting one another; it is also the scene of the end of an age. As the battle continues, the collapse of the old order becomes increasingly visible beside the courage of the warriors.

Iran's defeat at al-Qadisiyyah had consequences far beyond a single battlefield. The road toward the country's important centers was opened to the invading forces, and the Sasanian government could no longer gather scattered forces into a single front as it had before.

After al-Qadisiyyah, important cities and regions came under attack one after another. The fall of Ctesiphon and the loss of the political center dealt a severe blow to imperial authority. Yazdegerd III was forced away from the center of government and moved east in search of a possibility of resistance.

In this section, the Shahnameh emphasizes not only armies and military formations but also the sorrow of Iran's lost splendor. The heroes who had accompanied earlier generations on battlefields now face the end of a world built over centuries.

Within the structure of the narrative, al-Qadisiyyah is a point of rupture. The Sasanians continue to resist for a time afterward, but they can no longer restore the empire of the past. The story now moves toward final collapse and then toward the cultural and historical legacy of Iran in a new age.

58.title: Part 58: Ctesiphon and the End of Sasanian Splendor
58.prose:
Ctesiphon, the magnificent capital of the Sasanians, no longer possessed its former security and authority after successive defeats. The city that had been a center of rule, treasure, and royal splendor for centuries now stood before an army advancing from the western borders and shaking the political structure of Iran.

The palaces and iwans of Ctesiphon were remnants of an age in which the Sasanian kings had extended their power across the region. Here architectural magnificence and political power were intertwined. Yet the Shahnameh reminds us that no structure is beyond the turning of time, and splendor founded upon political power can suddenly decline.

With the loss of Ctesiphon, Yazdegerd III could no longer govern the country from a strong center as earlier kings had done. He was forced to leave the capital and move east to gather forces and preserve the throne. Each new city was both a refuge and a reminder that the empire's territory was becoming smaller.

Sasanian wealth and treasures also acquired a different meaning. What had once been signs of power and splendor now faced the danger of plunder and dispersal. In its epic vision, the Shahnameh presents this change as the gradual collapse of a world that generations had fought to build.

The Iwan of Khosrow assumes symbolic importance in this account. The building that embodied imperial power now stood against the passage of time and historical change. Its magnificence could remain, but those who possessed that magnificence could no longer control the country's destiny as before.

The fall of Ctesiphon did not mean that all resistance ended immediately. Yazdegerd and groups of Iranians continued to resist in different parts of the country, and for a time the hope of restoring Sasanian power remained alive. But the political center had been lost, and rebuilding the former empire had become extremely difficult.

For this reason, Ctesiphon at the end of the Sasanian narrative is more than a city; it is a sign of the end of an age. From here the story reaches Yazdegerd's final efforts and then his death. What survives from Ctesiphon and the Sasanians, however, is not only ruin: the memory of Iran, its language, culture, and historical stories also pass from this age to later generations.
